title: JavaScript: Giving Our Game a Brain
subtitle: Let's Teach Our Game How to Think

scenes.name: Lesson opener
scenes.visual: Lesson card: 'LESSON 4 · JAVASCRIPT' gold tile, 'Giving Our Game a Brain'.
scenes.onScreen: LESSON 4 · JavaScript: Giving Our Game a Brain

scenes.name: Looks are not enough
scenes.visual: The IDE preview shows the styled page from Lesson 3 with its empty grid. The cursor clicks the empty grid: nothing happens (a small 'click' ripple, nothing else). Three flat icon chips appear: RESPOND (hand), REMEMBER (box), DECIDE (signpost). Then a gold 'brain' outline settles over the grid.
scenes.sfx: Click with no response (a dull tick), pops for the chips.

lines.text: Welcome back, creators! Our game looks amazing. But try clicking a card...
Nothing happens. In fact, there are no cards yet!
Looks alone don't make a game. A game needs to respond, to remember, and to decide.
That's the job of JavaScript. JavaScript gives our game its behaviour. You can think of it as the game's brain.

scenes.name: Create script.js and link it
scenes.visual: New file → 'script.js' typed → JS icon appears; the sidebar now lists index.html, style.css, script.js (brief glow on all three). In index.html, under the stylesheet link, <script src="script.js" defer></script> types in. 'defer' animation: a page outline is read top to bottom with a progress line, and only when it reaches the end does a gold JS tile run.
scenes.onScreen: script.js · <script src="script.js" defer></script> · defer = read the page first, then run

lines.text: Click the new file button, type script dot J S, and press Enter.
lines.caption: Click the new file button, type script.js, and press Enter.

lines.text: Our project now has three files.
Back in index dot html, under the stylesheet link, we add a script tag. Its source attribute says script dot J S.
lines.caption: Back in index.html, under the stylesheet link, we add a <script> tag. Its src attribute says script.js.

lines.text: The word defer means: first finish reading the whole page, and then run the JavaScript. That way, every element is ready when our code looks for it.

scenes.name: Variables
scenes.visual: Concept stage (deep green). A labelled box 'moves' opens and a 0 drops in. The 0 is swapped for 1, 2, 3 with little pops. Code at 40px: let moves = 0; let score = 0; (labelled 'teaching example'). Then the real game variables from script.js appear as a shelf of labelled boxes: firstCard (empty/null), secondCard (null), lockBoard (false), moves (0), matchedPairs (0), totalPairs (6), seconds (0). Each lights up when named.
scenes.onScreen: let moves = 0; · TEACHING EXAMPLE · null = empty
scenes.transition: Boxes line up into an array.

lines.text: Let's meet our first big idea: variables.
A variable is like a labelled box, where the computer keeps information.
Let moves equal zero creates a box called moves, and puts zero inside.
lines.caption: let moves = 0; creates a box called moves, and puts zero inside.

lines.text: Later, we can change what's inside. When the player makes a move, moves becomes one, then two, then three.
Our game uses variables to remember everything important.
First card and second card remember the two cards the player has turned over. They start as null, which means empty.
lines.caption: firstCard and secondCard remember the two cards the player has turned over. They start as null, which means empty.

lines.text: Lock board remembers whether the player has to wait.
lines.caption: lockBoard remembers whether the player has to wait.

lines.text: Moves and matched pairs keep count. Total pairs remembers how many pairs we need, and seconds counts the time.
lines.caption: moves and matchedPairs keep count. totalPairs remembers how many pairs we need, and seconds counts the time.

scenes.name: Arrays
scenes.visual: const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; at 40px (teaching example). Six mini number cards slot into a tray with numbered compartments. Then the real createDeck code: the tray duplicates (copy slides down), the two trays merge into one of 12, and pairs are joined by thin lines.
scenes.camera: Locked, with a pan along the tray.
scenes.sfx: Tick per slot, whoosh on the duplicate.

lines.text: Next big idea: arrays.
An array stores several values together, in order, inside square brackets.
Here, the numbers array holds one, two, three, four, five and six.
But a memory game needs pairs! So our create deck function uses the numbers twice, joined into one bigger array.
lines.caption: But a memory game needs pairs! So our createDeck function uses the numbers twice, joined into one bigger array.

lines.text: Now every number has a partner. Twelve cards, six pairs.

scenes.name: Functions
scenes.visual: A flat recipe card labelled sayHello() with its steps. The teaching-example code appears; 'sayHello();' is called and the IDE console bar opens showing 'Hello, creator!'. Then five function cards from script.js are dealt in a row; each flips over to show its one-line job and a tiny animation (createDeck: 1–6 doubles; shuffle: cards swap; createCard: a card assembles; buildBoard: cards fill the grid; flipCard: a card turns).
scenes.camera: Pan across the row of function cards.
scenes.sfx: Card deal sounds, a flip per reveal.

lines.text: Big idea number three: functions.
A function is a set of instructions with a name. We write it once, and use it again and again.
This function is called say hello. When we call it, it writes, Hello, creator! in the console.
lines.caption: This function is called sayHello. When we call it, it writes "Hello, creator!" in the console.

lines.text: Our game has lots of helpful functions.
Create deck makes the pairs of numbers.
lines.caption: createDeck makes the pairs of numbers.

lines.text: Shuffle mixes them into a random order, just like shuffling real cards.
lines.caption: shuffle mixes them into a random order, just like shuffling real cards.

lines.text: Create card builds one card, with its green back and its number front.
lines.caption: createCard builds one card, with its green back and its number front.

lines.text: Build board puts all the cards into the game grid.
lines.caption: buildBoard puts all the cards into the game grid.

lines.text: And flip card turns a card over when the player clicks it.
lines.caption: And flipCard turns a card over when the player clicks it.

scenes.name: Events
scenes.visual: Three event icons (click, key, list choice). Then the real line card.addEventListener("click", () => flipCard(card)); at 34px, with labels under each part: 'listen for' · 'a click' · 'then run'. Right side: a card. The cursor clicks it; a gold signal travels along a connector from the card into the code, and the card flips.
scenes.transition: Two cards appear for the decision.

lines.text: But how does the game know when we click? With events.
An event is something that happens on a webpage, like a click, a key press, or a choice from a list.
This line tells each card: listen for a click. And when a click happens, run flip card for this card.
lines.caption: This line tells each card: listen for a click. And when a click happens, run flipCard for this card.

lines.text: Click... and flip card runs. The card turns over!
lines.caption: Click... and flipCard runs. The card turns over!

scenes.name: if and else
scenes.visual: Code at 34px: the if/else teaching snippet. Two lanes side by side: LEFT, a 3 and a 3 → YES → green, cards stay up; RIGHT, a 3 and a 5 → NO → red shake, cards turn back. A flat signpost splits the path. '===' is enlarged with the label 'exactly the same?'.
scenes.onScreen: if ( ... === ... ) · YES → match · else → no match
scenes.sfx: Match chime on the left, gentle buzz on the right.

lines.text: Our game also needs to make decisions. For that, we use if, and else.
This if statement asks a question: is the number on the first card the same as the number on the second card?
If the answer is yes, the cards match, and they stay face up.
Else, if the answer is no, they don't match, and they turn back over.
Three equals signs mean: are these exactly the same?

scenes.name: The DOM
scenes.visual: The HTML from Lesson 2 becomes a tree of boxes (DOM tree). A magnifying-glass cursor runs document.getElementById("gameGrid") and finds and lights up the #gameGrid box, with the id in the HTML highlighted too. Then createElement("button") produces a card and appendChild drops it into the grid; it repeats quickly until 12 cards fill the preview.
scenes.camera: Pan from the tree to the preview.
scenes.transition: The filled grid shrinks to the end card.

lines.text: One more idea: the DOM. That's how JavaScript sees our webpage: as a family of elements it can find, and change.
Document dot get element by I D finds an element using its I D. Here, it finds the game grid we made in HTML.
lines.caption: document.getElementById finds an element using its id. Here, it finds the game grid we made in HTML.

lines.text: Remember when we gave our elements I Ds? This is why!
lines.caption: Remember when we gave our elements ids? This is why!

lines.text: Then, create element makes a brand new button for each card, and append child adds it into the grid.
lines.caption: Then, createElement makes a brand new button for each card, and appendChild adds it into the grid.

lines.text: That's how the cards appear. JavaScript builds them for us!

scenes.name: Closing
scenes.visual: Recap chips appear one by one: VARIABLES · ARRAYS · FUNCTIONS · EVENTS · IF/ELSE · DOM. The chips snap into puzzle pieces that do not quite connect yet. End card: 'Next: Making the Game Work'.
scenes.onScreen: Next: The Magic Behind Number Match

lines.text: Your game now has a brain!
We have learned about variables, arrays, functions, events, decisions, and the DOM.
But we haven't connected all those ideas into the complete game just yet.
Let's do that in our next lesson!
